_comment: The page's opening URL and trick gallery. site/record/record.py records other parsers' answers for these inputs into site/recorded.json; site/build.py renders them. The explanations are HTML.

cards.title: Short addresses
cards.explain: Browsers read IPv4 addresses with missing parts, as the old inet_aton did, so 127.1 is 127.0.0.1. A parser that keeps the text lets it past a blocklist of 127.0.0.1, and the system's resolver usually connects to loopback anyway.

cards.title: Hex addresses
cards.explain: Parts in hex (or octal, with a leading 0) are numbers too. A check that looks for internal addresses as text misses them; Hrefine says the host is an IPv4 address, whatever it looks like.

cards.title: One big number
cards.explain: A whole address as one decimal number, 127 × 2²⁴ + 1. Python, Java, and Go keep it as text, and the browser reads loopback.

cards.title: Backslashes
cards.explain: Browsers treat \ as / in http and https URLs. Python and Go find no host here at all, so a host check has nothing to stop, and the browser goes to evil.example.

cards.title: Open redirects
cards.explain: A server checks that a next parameter is a path on its own site, and Python, Java's URL, C#, Go, and curl all say it is. The browser, resolving it against the page, goes to evil.example.

cards.title: Who's the host?
cards.explain: Everything before @ is a user name, so the host is evil.example. Parsers agree; the trap is people, and checks like startsWith("https://good.example").

cards.title: Fragments with @
cards.explain: Everything after # is the fragment, so the host is evil.example. Parsers agree; a check that takes the text after the last @ reads good.example.

cards.title: Tabs and newlines
cards.explain: Browsers drop tabs and newlines anywhere in a URL, so this host ends in .evil.example. Strict parsers refuse it, which is safe only if nothing downstream reads it the browser's way.

cards.title: javascript:, hidden
cards.explain: A filter looking for javascript: misses it, but browsers drop the tab and run the script. Check the parsed scheme, never the text.

cards.title: Look-alike letters
cards.explain: The first letter is Cyrillic а, so browsers send xn--pple-43d.com, which isn't apple.com. Some parsers keep the Unicode, so a check and a request can see different names. This is the long-known IDN homograph trick.

cards.title: Dots that aren't dots
cards.explain: Browsers read the ideographic full stop 。 as a dot, so this is a name under evil.example. Parsers without IDNA see one odd label, and a check for names ending in .evil.example misses it.

cards.title: Protocol-relative
cards.explain: It starts with /, so it looks like a path on your own site, but // starts a host. Every parser agrees; the trap is checks like startsWith("/").

cards.title: Too many slashes
cards.explain: Browsers and curl skip extra slashes and find evil.example. Python, Java, and Go see no host, and C# refuses it.
